div.p: In recent years mechatronic systems have evolved towards a new generation of cyber-physical systems. Technology has shifted from mechanical control systems towards electronic control systems, which introduces a fast growing complexity. The use of multi-core processors and virtualization techniques on embedded systems tackles this complexity by decoupling software from hardware. Virtualization introduces a hierarchical scheduling structure, where hard real-time behavior must be guaranteed within the level of guest operating system scheduler and at the level of the hypervisor scheduler. This paper gives the current state of the art of schedulability analysis methodologies for hierarchical scheduling techniques and its application in real-time hypervisors
• Redundancy: the possibility to implement software redundancy on a single platform.

Transferring virtualization technology onto embedded systems is not straightforward. The needs of embedded systems differ from those of servers, and a hypervisor for embedded systems must address these needs. Embedded systems generally require real-time guarantees that have to be taken into

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: Virtualization technology is widely used in personal computing, cloud computing and in server infrastructures. It enables the support of multiple concurrent execution environments on a single hardware platform and the dynamic allocation of hardware resources to each of these environments. The middle-ware between the hardware and the guest operating systems, is called the hypervisor. It manages the physical devices and the guest operating systems, or virtual machines (VMs) that execute on top of that physical hardware. In this context virtualization offers a number of benefits [34]:
• Server consolidation: running multiple operating systems temporal and spacial isolated from each other on a single hardware platform.
• Heterogeneous operating systems: the support for running diverse operating systems concurrently on the same hardware.
• Dynamic resource allocation: resources can be added to or removed from the virtual machines based on the applications needs.

Due to the shift from mechanical control towards electronic control in mechatronic environments, embedded systems be-come more complex. Because of this transition, more functionally can be added to the control logic. This evolution has a downside. Reliability and robustness level of mechanic controllers is harder to realize in software (on electronic controllers). This implies that additional logic has to be added to the controllers to be conform to safety regulations [18]. This results in increasing complexity and cost. These complex real-time systems are making the shift from isolated embedded systems towards cyber-physical systems (CPS), i.e. physically isolated hosts evolve towards multi-core computing platforms shared by multiple systems. Analyzing such complex systems, requires for new techniques to decrease or handle the complexity.

In the domain of embedded real-time systems [17], popularity of virtualization is growing. Virtualization technology can be used to facilitate the design of embedded systems by deploying the logic of different subsystems in separate virtual machines on the same hardware. In combination with the multi-core technique, this offers the designer the capability of centralizing and decentralizing software to hardware (Figure 1). Applying this on embedded systems, and therefore executing multiple real-time operating systems on one controller, has significant advantages:
• Portability: the ability to easily port designs to hardware platforms.
• Partitioning: secure partitioning of guest operating systems.

• Integration: easy integration of new applications onto existing platforms and vice versa. account when applying virtualization technology. The goal of this paper is highlight the gaps between current schedulability analysis techniques for real-time VMs and the current implementations of virtualization on embedded systems. We also indicate how to modify these techniques to conform to the requirements of real-time embedded applications.

Section II lists the advantages and disadvantages of the different techniques for executing an OS in a virtualized environment. Section III gives an overview of schedulability analysis theories for a hierarchical scheduling structure, focusing on multiprocessor support. In Section IV the current status of implementation of virtualization on embedded systems is reviewed. In Section V, the gaps between the theories and the implementations are summed up together with the limitations of current theories to support the requirements of real-time applications. Section VI presents the conclusions and is followed by our vision on the future of virtualization in embedded systems in Section VII.

div.head: II. TYPES OF VIRTUALIZATION
div.p: This paper focuses on hypervisor-based virtualization. Hypervisor-based virtualization enables to host several guest operating systems (VMs) on a single hardware platform. Each one of these guest operating systems can run its own applications, as if it owns the allocated resource of the host. In reality, however, it is the hypervisor that allocates shares of those resources to the VMs.
There are different ways to implement virtualization. Common techniques are full virtualization and para-virtualization [1].

Full virtualization provides a full abstraction of the underlying physical hardware and creates a complete virtual system on which the guest OS can run. In other words, the guest OS is not aware of being executed in virtualized environment. The advantage of this approach is that it enables complete decoupling of software and hardware. Full virtualization provides complete isolation of different VMs, leading to strong security. The disadvantage of this approach is the required hardware support. All CPU sensitive instructions must be privileged instructions to prevent VMs from making adjustments in the physical hardware [31]. The privileged instructions of the VMs are trapped-and-emulated, which results in performance loss.

Para-virtualization provides each VM with an abstraction of the hardware that is similar, but not identical, to the underlying hardware. Hence, para-virtualization requires modifications to the guest OS. As a result, the guest OS is aware of being executed in a virtual environment. The performance of a paravirtualized OS is near native performance. Hypercalls are used to request the hypervisor's services. These hypercalls can be used as a communication channel between the guest OS and the hypervisor.

For embedded systems, both techniques are used. Paravirtualization has some more advantages in terms of efficiency (reduction of overhead [21]), and in terms of run-time flexibility because of the explicit communication between guest OS and hypervisor. The major drawback is the need to port the guest OS, which involves modifications to critical kernel parts. If technical or other issues preclude this for an OS, it is not possible at all to host the OS.

div.head: III. HIERARCHICAL SCHEDULABILITY ANALYSIS
div.p: Real-time scheduling requires analysis to prove that tasks can be executed before a deadline. This schedulability analysis makes use of the Worst Case Execution Time (WCET) of the tasks. When implementing virtualization for embedded systems, a hierarchical scheduling structure is created. The virtual CPUs (VCPUs) are scheduled on the physical CPU(s) (PCPU), and the real-time tasks are scheduled on the VCPUs (Figure 2). Both scheduling levels must honour real-time guarantees to achieve the real-time guarantees for the whole system. The established approach of the schedulability analysis [25] is no longer applicable to this scheduling problem.

The distinction between the virtualization scheduling structure and the hierarchical scheduling structure is subtle. Theories to analyze hierarchical scheduling structures are adopted to tackle the schedulability analysis for real-time VMs and the theories are modified based on feedback from the implementation of virtualization on embedded systems. To fulfill the virtualization requirements, the communication at run-time between both scheduling levels must be as sparse as possible to respect to isolation and security between the VMs and the hypervisor. In full virtualization, the hypervisor has no information about the scheduling and task behavior in the VMs. In para-virtualization, the VMs can exchange information with the hypervisor, but the benefit of the communication must Fig. 2. Visual representation of a hierarchical scheduling structure on a multi-core platform be significant compared to the overhead of processing the information [16].

Scheduling assigns resources according to a scheduling policy in order to process workloads. The scheduling can be characterized by a scheduling model that consists of three elements: a resource model, a scheduling algorithm, and a workload model [33]. A hierarchical scheduling framework supports hierarchical resource sharing under different scheduling algorithms for different scheduling services. It can be represented as a tree, or a hierarchy, of nodes. Each node represents a scheduling model and a resource that is allocated from a parent node to its children (Figure 2). A resource allocation from parent to child is characterized by a scheduling interface. The interface captures the contract of real-time guarantees between parent and child (schedulability analysis).
In the remainder of the section we review the schedulability analysis of hierarchical scheduling structures for single-and for multiprocessor platforms.

div.head: A. Single processor approaches
div.p: In [11], [12] a hierarchical scheduling framework was presented to schedule real-time applications in a 2-level hierarchy. The interface is specified in a uniform slow resource, or a fractional resource. This resource is always available only at a fraction of total utilization. A parent node supplies a fraction to a child node, and the child node calculate the fraction it demands. The schedulability analysis of each realtime application can be done traditionally, the fraction can easily be derived from the result of the analysis. However, the method does not include the timing requirements of the applications. This leads to interaction between child and parent node about task-level deadline information.

In [29] the static resource partition model has been introduced as a first resource partition model. In [14], the boundeddelay resource partition model is described for a hierarchical scheduling framework. This resource partition model describes a behavior of a partitioned resource that is available at its full capacity at some times but not at all other times. However, even though a child node runs over a partitioned resource, its schedulability is analyzed as if it runs over a fractional resource. The partitioned resource model only holds when the maximum output jitter of each task of the child node, is no less then the time when no resources are allocated to the child model. Thus, the scheduling algorithm of a child node is required to handle this difference by applying the notion of virtual time scheduling.

The Periodic Resource Model (PRM) [33] tackles this problem by providing a resource model that gives the strict number of computing units the component can use during a period. This resource model includes the task-level requirements, which implies that a child node only reckons with the given partition of the resource model in the schedulability analysis. For both rate-monotonic (RM) and earliest deadline first (EDF) scheduling algorithms, the number of computation units can be calculated for a given period. The Explicit Deadline Periodic resource model (EDP) [13] generalizes the PRM model by using explicit deadlines (deadline ≤ period).

div.head: B. Multiprocessor approaches
div.p: Because of the multi-core integration into embedded systems, schedulability analysis for a multi-level hierarchical multiprocessor structure is the logical response. The first resource model, where a child node can have more than one processor, is the Multiprocessor Periodic Resource Model (MPR) [32]. The interface has similarities with the PRM interface, only the computation units are consumed concurrently. ḿ represents the maximum number of computation units consumed at one time unit. The tasks in the task sets are independent and a task can not be parallelized. The interface includes timing requirements. For task-level scheduling, the global EDF scheduling algorithm is used. To perform the schedulability analysis at a higher level, each interface is transformed into ḿ periodic tasks with the period of the interface. The sum of these task's WCET is equal to computation units of the interface. By setting the same period for each processor of a child node and the aggregation of an unique amount of computation units can lead to a pessimistic analysis.

In [3], [4] the Parallel Supply Function (PSF) makes it possible to have different periods between the processors within a child node. This interface is designed to strictly capture the amount of resource supplied to a child for very general supply mechanisms, which are not necessarily periodic. In this approach there is no reasoning concerning the computation of the interface parameters that guarantee the schedulability of a real-time application. [24] describes the Bounded-Delay Multipartition model (BDM). The proposed interface is based on the bounded-delay function, in which the maximum time given where no resources are allocated to the child node. A set of resource fractions, with corresponding parallelism factor, is given. This allows the designer to set the parameters of the child model, balanced between resource usage and flexibility.

The Generalized Multiprocessors Periodic Resource model (GMPR) [5], is an extension of MPR model. In this model multiple values of computation units are calculated with a given period. Each value of computation units is associated with a number of virtual processors. With an optimization algorithm, the best fitting value is chosen for a specific task set, which reduces the resource overhead caused by the interface.

div.head: IV. REAL-TIME HYPERVISORS
div.p: The realization of a virtualized environment with real-time guarantees requires modifications to existing hypervisors, or in some cases a totally new hypervisor. Research on realtime hypervisors with the support for scheduling multiple VMs with real-time requirements is limited, especially on a multicore platform. In [39], [23], [10], [2], [22], [40], [28] the authors focus on a VM with real-time requirements (RTVM) in combination with VMs without real-time requirements. Our focus is on hypervisors with support for multiple real-time VMs. Below we first describe the different implementations for a single-core processor and then for a multi-core processor.

In [26] the SEDF scheduler of Xen [7] is modified to support real-time VMs by adding priority based scheduling. A realtime VM is limited to one real-time task to guarantee correct timing behavior. In [27] this limitation is removed. In this case however the VMs are limited to one VCPU and not allowed to migrate from one core to another. The authors presented a design procedure to calculate the optimal time-slice and period for a VM under deadline monotonic scheduling. The research included network I/O in a seperated VM (DomN), where incoming/outgoing packets are processed and passed through the designated RTVM.

In [38] the PRM is implemented with the L4/Fiasco microkernel as a hypervisor on a single core hardware platform. The number of computation units Θ is calculated online. In other words, when a new task is generated in a real-time VM, the new interface is calculated. This requires para-virtualization to inform the hypervisor about the new real-time tasks. The process to recalculate and assign to interface results in a large overhead. These overheads depend on the number of VMs and scales linearly. However, this overhead only occurs with a task set change. The authors do not propose an analysis of schedulability at hypervisor-level.

Another implementation of the PRM is RT-Xen [35]. Here different server mechanisms are evaluated on real-time performance. The authors conclude that the deferrable server outperforms the other. In theory, the budget assigned to a VM via the PRM interface is quite rigid. The deferrable server relaxes this by saving the remaining budget when the guest OS is idle. This budget can be used until the next period when the guest OS become active.

Proteus [20] is a full virtualization hypervisor for Pow-erPC405. This work supports multiple VMs with real-time tasks on a single core processor. Multiple systems with different processor frequencies are consolidated to one system through virtualization. First, the utilization of each system is calculated as if it were executing on the slowest system. Based on the summation of the utilization factors, the minimum speed of the target system is determined. The goal of this research is to schedule real-time VMs with full virtualization. In [15] the Proteus hypervisor is extended to a multi-core hypervisor. It supports full virtualization and para-virtualization.

In [37] the single-core hypervisor RT-Xen is implemented on a multi-core platform. This is realized with the deterministic MPR interface (DMPR). Via the DMPR interface ḿ -1 virtual CPUs are dedicated and one virtual CPU is partially dedicated. The dedicated VCPUs are pinned on the PCPUs without being scheduled, and the partially dedicated VCPUs are scheduled on the remaining PCPUs by the hypervisor scheduler. Results shows a decreasing amount of cache misses because the majority of the PCPUs schedules only one VCPU.

In [36] RT-Xen is modified to support multi-core platforms. Multiple models are supported: MPR, DMPR, MSF, GMPR. The defferable and periodic server mechanism are tested in cooperation with the global EDF scheduler. The MPR resource model is used in the empirical evaluation. The combination of the global EDF scheduling algorithm as hypervisor scheduler with VMs as defferable servers and the partitioned EDF algorithm as task-level scheduler, results in the lowest deadline misses. At this moment, RT-Xen [36] is the only hypervisor with the support of real-time multiprocessor hierarchical scheduling structure.

We observe that real-time virtualization with the support of multiple RTVMs is still in an early stage of development. The current focus is on scheduling independent real-time tasks in virtualized environment.

div.head: V. DISCUSSION
div.p: In this section, we want to point to two issues that arise with current research and formulate some open questions that are in our opinion, relevant to the problem of schedulability analysis for virtualized systems.

The first issue concerns the gap between current methods for schedulability analysis of a hierarchical scheduling structure (Section III) and the problem context of real-time hypervisors (Section IV). This gap is evidenced in the following points:

• A resource model should be flexible in the sense that it allows, even when the system is online, adjustment of the parameters of the interfaces. In much of the current research the interfaces are assigned and are not changed during execution. In [38] a first step to address this issue was taken, but no analysis for hypervisor-level scheduling has been undertaken. In [16] the remaining budget of VMs is divided over the other VMs, based on VM priority. The disadvantage is the extra overhead for the recalculation of the budgets and the communication between hypervisor and VMs. • The theory of schedulability analysis takes into account such elements as overhead of the scheduler at tasklevel and hypervisor-level and the effect of caches [30], [37]. However, the performance results of the real-time hypervisor are not taken into account. • In real-time multi-core schedulability analysis, different simulation softwares exist [8], [6]. A first adaptation towards a multi-level hierarchical scheduling structure is realized in [9]. Further research is needed to simulate a multiprocessor platform with the support of the different resource models. The second issue concerns the limitations of current schedulability analysis for real-time applications that run in a virtualized environment. The limitations are:

• The lack of support of network and other I/O device dependencies in the interface. Tasks often depend on input data and/or send output data. When these resources are globally or locally shared, different synchronization protocols are required to share resource at both levels.

In [19] resources are shared at task-level and systemlevel, but the implementation of the hierarchical scheduling framework is not done through virtualization and requires extra communication between both levels. • The lack of timing analysis of tasks executing in a virtualized environment. When an OS is running as a virtual machine, its privileged instructions are emulated by the hypervisor. The emulation service is requested through interrupt (full virtualization) or via a hypercall (para-virtualization). Both have an impact on the executing time of the privileged instruction. Comparing to full virtualization, para-virtualization handles these instruction faster. In [15] the average speedup of the paravirtualization technique, compared to full virtualization, is analyzed for the Proteus hypervisor. The emulation of the instructions has a direct effect on the WCET of a task in a real-time application of the guest OS. These limitations impact on the link between the experimental testing environments with generated task sets and the use of case studies from the industry.

div.head: VI. CONCLUSION
div.p: As mechatronic systems continue to grow in complexity, we believe that applying the virtualization technique on embedded systems can reduce the complexity of analyzing the network of embedded systems of such a mechatronic system. This approach is a hot topic in state of the art research on embedded systems. Current solutions show a lack of feedback between the schedulability theories and the implementations of the virtualization technique on embedded systems. In addition, current theories are limited in there support of real-time applications running in virtualized embedded systems. This results in major challenges for the schedulability theories.

div.head: VII. FUTURE WORK
div.p: This concludes that there are limitations to the applicability of current schedulability theory to the implementations of virtualization on embedded systems. To lift these limitations, three major topics must be addressed.

The first is the need to add an extra layer to the development process. This layer consists of the simulation of virtualized embedded systems. We believe that simulation can significantly enrich the development process. The second topic is the traceability of modifications to real-time hypervisors to the schedulability theory. This improves the applicability and correctness of current theories. The third topic is the support of I/O and other task dependencies in the schedulability theories. Realization of these working points would substantially bridge the gap between schedulability theory and the use of virtualization on multi-core embedded systems.

Any change in software allocation results in going through the last steps of the development process again. The ECUs can be changed and the VCUs can be allocated to other ECUs without modifying the software.
